 CSCI/DASC 6010: Big Data Analytics and Management
Spring 2026
Final Project
1 Introduction
The goals of the final project are to use the tools & techniques you’ve learned in this class to analyze a dataset
that interests you, to tell a compelling story with visualizations, and to do something cool/meaningful with
data. The project must:
• Use or develop a dataset, and report empirical results or analyses with the dataset (it may use any
type of open-source or widely available free software), or
• Propose a new method relevant for big data management and analysis.
One place to get inspiration for project ideas is from TED Talks, e.g., How the US is destroying young
people’s future by Scott Galloway (he has other interesting talks), The best stats you’ve ever seen or Let my
dataset change your mindset by Hans Rosling (he also has other interesting talks).
You can choose to emphasize:
• Implementing and developing algorithms and features.
• Defining a new analysis task.
• Collect and explore a new dataset to address research hypotheses about it.
• Different projects will have different balances of these three things.
The key requirement is to investigate, analyze, and come to research findings about new methods, or insights
about previously existing methods.
This course does not have a final exam. The final project is the focus for the final part of the course.
The project will be completed in groups of two to three students. I encourage groups of three students,
which often works well.
2 Final project presentations
Here is a sample outline for your presentation. There are different possible ways to structure it (for example,
if you can, you can weave related work into the other sections), but I suggest you follow this outline.
• Introduction: explain the problem, motivate it (why is it important?), and briefly describe your
approach. State a research question that your project seeks to answer: what are you trying to learn
from this research project? You may also report some of your results without discussing the details of
your method.
• Related work: explain what other approaches have been proposed by others to address this problem.
Cite specific instances of previous work.
• Data: Describe in detail the dataset that you are using so that the audience can reproduce your work,
e.g., answer as many questions as possible from Datasheets for datasets (available from ACM DL and
arXiv).
• Method: Describe your approach to handling the problem. This should include any models you used
and any modeling assumptions you made. If you’ve developed new models for this project, you may
even want to split a description/analysis of your models into its own section.
1
• Results: Describe the experiments you ran and identify your baseline method(s). Include the results
you achieved with the various methods you are comparing. This section will probably also include
some figures that succinctly summarize your results. Analyze your results (including your models). If
you did exploratory analysis or a significant amount of feature engineering, your analysis may merit its
own section. After reading this section (and your dataset and methods), an interested reader should
be able to replicate your experiments and results.
• Discussion and Future Work: discuss any implications of your analysis for the problem as a whole,
and what are the next steps for future work. Any other concluding remarks should go here.
Some things to remember:
• PRESENT CLEARLY. A good presentation is direct, unambiguous and describes all stages of the
work in complete – but not superfluous – detail. You must provide this, while not causing confusion
to the viewer. The quality of your presentation will affect your grade.
• All plots, figures, and tables must have a title, labeled axes and a caption. There should be no confusion
about what you’re trying to express, or why the plot was included.
• Do not include multiple figures that all convey the same information. Be succinct.
• Avoid redundancy. Do not describe the same component of your work twice.
• Do not include much code in your presentation. If your approach contains a new algorithm you
developed, it may be appropriate for you to include its pseudocode, but do not copy and paste code
from your editor. Do not include well-known algorithms like the perceptron training algorithm. (If
you feel like you need to, instead include a citation to the literature that describes the algorithm, and
provide a brief English description of what it does.)
• You may include back-references to things you’ve already discussed. Avoid forward references.
• Provide a title for your presentation.
Creating a presentation is like composing a piece of art. Be deliberate in your choice of what to include,
when to include it and how to express it. For example, don’t include every plot you generated; pick the ones
that best demonstrate your results. Work on the clarity of your presentation. At the end of the day, your
presentation is all the viewer has to generate an opinion about your work. You don’t want good work to be
obscured by poor presentation delivery.
